title: In Joel 2 What Does The Imagery Of Locusts And A Great Army Teach Us About Gods Judgment
paragraphs: Understanding Joel 2: The Locusts, the Army, and God's Judgment

The book of Joel is one of the most vivid prophetic texts in the Old Testament. In chapter 2, the prophet describes an overwhelming invasion—first by locusts, then by a great army. These two images are deeply intertwined, serving as both literal and figurative warnings of God's coming judgment. But what exactly do these vivid pictures teach us about the nature of God's judgment, His character, and our response? Let’s explore the passage and unpack its rich theological message.
The Locusts: A Picture of Devastation
Joel begins by describing a plague of locusts that devastates the land of Judah. The locusts are depicted not merely as an ecological disaster, but as a direct act of divine judgment:

A day of darkness and gloominess, a day of clouds and thick darkness! As the dawn spread upon the mountains, a great people and a strong; there hath not been ever the like, neither shall be any more after them, even to the years of many generations. -
Joel 2:2 ASV

The locust swarm is described as "a great people and a strong," symbolizing an unstoppable force. Throughout the Old Testament, locusts are often used as instruments of God's judgment (cf. Exodus 10:12 ASV). Here, their destructive power illustrates the totality of God’s judgment against sin—nothing is left untouched or unaffected.
The Great Army: Literal or Figurative?
As the passage progresses, the imagery seems to shift from literal locusts to a metaphorical army:
They run like mighty men; they climb the wall like men of war; and they march every one on his ways, and they break not their ranks. -
Joel 2:7 ASV

Some interpreters see this as a continuation of the locust imagery, emphasizing their disciplined, destructive advance. Others see a prophetic foreshadowing of an invading human army (possibly the Babylonians), using the locusts as a metaphor. Both views underscore the seriousness of God’s judgment: whether through natural calamity or military conquest, God’s sovereign hand is at work.
The Purpose of Judgment: A Call to Repentance
The imagery is not meant merely to instill fear, but to drive the people to repentance. God’s judgment is always purposeful, aiming to bring His people back to Himself:

Yet even now, saith Jehovah, turn ye unto me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning: and rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto Jehovah your God; for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in lovingkindness, and repenteth him of the evil. -
Joel 2:12-13 ASV
In the midst of wrath, God’s mercy shines through. The invitation is clear: repentance opens the door to restoration. This is a consistent theme throughout Scripture (see also 2 Chronicles 7:14 ASV).
Christ in Joel 2: Judgment and Hope
From a Christ-centered perspective, Joel 2 not only warns of judgment but also points toward the ultimate outpouring of God’s Spirit:
And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh... -
Joel 2:28 ASV

This prophecy is fulfilled at Pentecost (see Acts 2:16-21 ASV), signifying the restoration and new life available to all who turn to Christ in faith. God’s judgment, therefore, is not His final word—His ultimate desire is redemption through Jesus Christ.
Key Insights for Today
God’s judgment is righteous and comprehensive: The locusts and army show that nothing escapes God's attention or justice (Romans 3:23 ASV).
God’s judgment is a call to repentance: His discipline is meant to turn hearts back to Him, not to destroy for destruction's sake (Hebrews 12:6 ASV).
God’s mercy is greater than His wrath: Even in judgment, He offers forgiveness and restoration to those who humbly repent (1 John 1:9 ASV).
God’s ultimate plan points to Christ: True restoration comes through faith in Jesus and the gift of the Holy Spirit.
